issues.text: The social cost of carbon range is reported using 95% confidence intervals, but the evaluator argues policymakers focus on single numbers and may fixate on the lower bound; the evaluator suggests using 90% intervals instead, which would be narrower and raise the reported lower bound. The evaluator frames this as a taste-based, normative comment.
issues.quote: it might be better to focus on a different, but equally conventional, bound: the 90% confidence interval.

issues.text: The paper lacks a comparison of its business-as-usual damage estimates across different pathways and integrated assessment models (IAMs), which the evaluator considers the primary request so readers can see how severe outcomes could be under alternative scenarios.
issues.quote: My primary request of the authors is to provide a comparison between [...] business-as-usual and the other pathways ahead.

issues.text: The number of lags used in the estimation is too short; the evaluator asks for at least 7 lags (the appendix goes only to 4), citing geophysical literature on solar cycles of similar or longer length.
issues.quote: increase the lags applied throughout (but most specifically in section 2.2) to at least 7 (the appendix goes to 4)

issues.text: The paper does not clearly characterise how far out of sample a 1C temperature change is, since the largest shock in the sample is only 0.3C, so the damage calibration relies on extrapolation the evaluator thinks should be made explicit.
issues.quote: A taste request is to characterize - up front - just how out-of-sample a 1C change truly is. The largest [change] in the sample is 0.3C.

issues.text: Calibrating response damages to the largest observed shock in the sample, rather than to a 1C change, is suggested as a way to add credibility to the headline estimates.
issues.quote: Calibrating response damages to this largest, but not particularly uncommon, shock might add to the credibility of the paper rather than take away from its message.
